content_metadata.description: A visual journey through the solar system that reveals the true scale of space and the limitations of traditional visualizations.

qAndA.question: Which two moons are shown to be bigger than the planet Mercury?
What is the average distance between asteroids in the Asteroid belt?
What is the name of the outermost region of the solar system where comets originate?
What is the speed limit of the rocket ship in the simulated flight?

qAndA.answer: The video contrasts the sizes of planets and their moons with the Sun, then shows the vast distances between them during the simulated space flight. This contrast highlights the immensity of space and the relative insignificance of individual celestial bodies.
qAndA.question: How does the video create a sense of awe at the scale of the solar system?

Text overlay: 'Distances are too big for both our senses and visualization. Actually, if we put both sizes and distances to scale... All we can see is shining dots, not very different from distant stars. Which is not really practical… And that is why all visualizations of the Solar System within a frame are more or less wrong. The only way to see the Solar System to scale is flying through it. Imagine you are in a rocket ship that goes up to 300,000,000 km/h. There'll be a lot of void, but we'll stop by each planet. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the Asteroid belt. Ceres is the biggest one, with a diameter of 950 km. Although there are millions of asteroids, the average distance between them is 1 million km, meaning that the belt is mostly empty. Sorry, there won't be a rodeo flight like in Star Wars… But still, it is to scale. Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, the kingdom of dwarf planets. Since 1992, more than 1000 objects bigger than 100 km have been discovered there. At approximately 8 billion km ends the Kuiper Belt. Beyond it are scattered-disc objects, the biggest known so far being Eris. Farther away begins the Oort Cloud, from 14 billion km to up to 3,000 billion km. This is where most comets hide, and where the Solar System ends.'

text_to_speech: This is the Solar System as we usually represent it. It's a useful representation, allowing us to see the entire system in a single frame. But both time and space are distorted here. First, time. The speeds of the 8 planets have been harmonized. Mercury is always the fastest, and Neptune the slowest. But Mercury should be 9 times faster than Neptune. Let's see what it's really like. Let's say 100 days last 1 second. See the difference? Now let's slow down time so that 4 days last 1 second. The planets spin much faster than they revolve around the Sun. The Earth spin in 1 day whereas it revolves around the Sun in 1 year. It rotates at a speed of 1600 kilometers per hour. Well, enough playing with time. In the same way as speeds, sizes have been harmonized. Let's try to really scale them up! Here you go! We can now see that several of the moons are roughly the same size as the first 4 planets. Actually Ganymede and Titan are both larger than Mercury. But wait! We forgot the sun... The Sun is so gigantic, that everything else seems tiny. The biggest problem in representing the Solar System is distance. Here, the Earth and Moon are in the right proportions. Now let's look at the actual distance between them... Remember that the Moon is by far the closest celestial body to Earth. For instance, Mars is at its closest 55.7 million kilometers from Earth. The distances are too great for our understanding. Actually, if we scale the sizes and distances to scale... All we see now are bright dots, merging with distant stars. And that's why representations of the Solar System are always more or less distorted. The only way to see the Solar System to scale is to fly through it. Imagine yourself in a rocket that can go at any speed. There will be a lot of void, but we'll stop at every planet. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt. Ceres is the largest of them, with a diameter of 950 km. Although there are millions of asteroids, the average distance between them is a million kilometers, The Belt is essentially empty. Sorry, no Star Wars-style space slalom. Of course, this flight is also distorted, as the planets are all aligned at the start. But it is to scale. Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, the realm of the dwarf planets. Since 1992, more than 1,000 objects more than 100 kilometers long have been discovered there. The Kuiper Belt ends about 8 billion kilometers from the Sun. Beyond are the scattered objects, the largest known to date being Eris. Even further away lies the Oort Cloud, between 14 billion and 3,000 billion kilometers away. This is where most comets hide, and where the Solar System ends. I hope you enjoyed your trip, Thanks for watching!

youtube_channel: After Effects Tips & Treats - by Julien Schickel
youtube_description:
The whole Solar System. Real Size. Real Scale. Real Time. Or about so...

-----

My 7 years old son asks me to do a space video, showing the "real" sizes of the Solar System.

While trying, I realize that it is actually impossible to show the System truly to scale, respecting sizes, distances, and times. That is something I've never realized so far.

I then started to change the video from "making a real size Solar System" to "explaining why it is impossible to make a real size Solar System."

So, here is the result!

-----

I made the video only on After Effects, using only surface pictures of the planets. If you're interested in a tutorial on how to do this kind of video, please ask for it in the comments.

Music by Bruno Delouzillière : https://soundcloud.com/bruno-dlz/sets

-----

French version here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJadtYf9-oA&t=24s

—

Lors of comments ask about the time scale of the last part of the video. It is indeed km/h, but at a Time scale of 1 day = 2 seconds.
